## The argument you are going to have

At some point this term you and a second coder will look at the same chat message and
disagree about what it is. Neither of you will be wrong, exactly.

Today is about seeing that argument coming, and building the codebook that settles it in
advance rather than at eleven at night in November.

You leave having sorted your own field notes into the easy half and the hard half.

## Two layers in every message

[Krippendorff, 2018]{.eyebrow}

- Content analysis separates two layers of meaning, and the split sits at the centre of
  codebook design
- **Manifest content:** what is explicitly present on the surface
- **Latent content:** the underlying meaning, which takes interpretation to reach
- Most first codebooks fail for one reason: they treat a latent variable as though it
  were manifest

## Manifest content

Features any trained coder can identify with high agreement:

- Does the message contain an `@` mention?
- Is it shorter than ten characters?
- Does it contain a known emote token?
- How many words is it?

These are countable almost mechanically. Coding them reliably is mostly a matter of writing
a clear rule once.

## Latent content

Features you cannot read off the surface:

- Is the message friendly or hostile?
- Is it directed at the streamer, or performing for the room?
- Is "first" a genuine claim or a running joke?
- Is the mood of chat, taken as a whole, celebratory or restless?

**Two careful coders can disagree about every one of these in good faith.**

## Why this is the argument for watching

- You cannot code latent content reliably until you have the interpretive framework that
  turns an impression into a defensible judgment
- That framework gets built by **watching**
- A coder who has spent twenty hours on live Twitch knows that a wall of one emote after a
  big play is celebration rather than noise
- They learned it by watching it happen, repeatedly, until the pattern was obvious
- Immersion is how latent content becomes codeable at all

## Your turn {.discuss}

- From your own field notes, name one thing you recorded that is clearly **manifest**
- Name one that is clearly **latent**, and say what a second coder might see differently
- For the latent one: what surface feature could stand in as evidence for it?

*Three minutes. Bring the hardest latent case to the room.*

## Sorting your notes

- Go through your field-notes document and mark every observation M or L
- Manifest items are candidate variables you could almost write today
- Latent items are candidate variables that will need **decision rules**
- A workable codebook usually mixes both: two or three manifest measures and one that takes
  real judgment
- If everything on your list is latent, your reliability check is going to hurt

## Sampling your observation

- You cannot watch all of Twitch, and you do not need to
- What you need is a **structured sample** of observation reflecting the range of the thing
  you will study
- Ten streams that are all large competitive-gaming channels teach you about large
  competitive-gaming channels
- About everything else, they will actively mislead you

## Match the range of your own source

- The class dataset spans a deliberate range: **50 channels** across the platform's volume
  distribution, gaming and non-gaming, heavily populated and nearly empty
- That range is the **principle**, not the assignment. Your observation should span the
  range of whatever source you settled on with the librarian.
- On Twitch that means big channels and small ones, gaming and Just Chatting and art
- On a subreddit it means busy threads and dead ones. On a news site, the front page and
  the pages nobody links to.
- Sample across **time** as well. A feed at peak and the same feed in a quiet hour are not
  the same room.

## Coverage beats volume

- **Twenty streams chosen to span the variety** will teach you more than fifty that are all
  the same kind
- Same principle as the wide literature search: see the shape of the whole conversation
- Same principle that governs statistical sampling later in the term
- Representativeness turns out to be a discipline that shows up at every stage of a study
- Observation is simply the first stage where it shows up

## When channels are actually live

[Figure 7.1, the collection week]{.eyebrow}

- Eight channels across the viewership distribution, November 18 to 24
- Large channels are live daily, for long stretches
- Small channels appear **once or twice all week**
- A randomly placed two-hour window intersects the big channels easily and catches the
  small ones only if you place it deliberately
- Scheduling your observation is itself a sampling decision

## The edge-case log

Some of what you observe will resist every category you are tempted to draw. Those moments
are not annoyances. They are the single most useful thing observation produces.

Keep an **edge-case log** alongside your field notes. For each case: log it, say what makes
it ambiguous, and list the ways a codebook could handle it.

## Four edge cases you will meet

- A message made **entirely of emotes**, with no words. Directed, broadcast, or a different
  kind of object altogether?
- **Copypasta**: a block every regular pastes without reading. Technically a message, and
  not in any normal sense written by that viewer.
- A message in a language you do not read
- An obvious **bot**, or a message grammatically addressed to the streamer but plainly a
  joke aimed at the room

## Edge cases become decision rules

- These are the raw material of the **decision rules** that make a codebook work
- The model prospectus carried an "unclassifiable" category. The edge-case log is how you
  find out what actually lands in it.
- A codebook written without one meets these messages for the first time during coding,
  when handling them is most expensive
- A codebook written with one has **already decided**, and coding becomes execution

## Knowing when to stop

Four signs immersion has done its job:

- New streams stop surprising you
- You can name three to five dimensions that clearly matter for your question
- Your edge-case log has enough entries to write rules from
- Your field notes repeat themselves, confirming patterns rather than turning up new ones

This is **saturation** again, the same idea the literature search used.

## What you walk away with

Structured listening leaves you four things:

- **Conceptual clarity** about what your variables mean in this particular medium
- A set of **candidate categories** for each one
- The beginnings of the **decision rules** for ambiguous cases
- Enough contextual knowledge to recognise when a surface feature is about to mislead you

Those four things are precisely the raw material of a codebook, which is what you build next.

## Before next time

- Finish your field notes and edge-case log: aim for **three or more observation sessions**
  spanning big, small, gaming, and non-gaming
- Mark every entry manifest or latent, and star the three you expect a second coder to
  fight you on
- Write **two or three candidate research questions** grounded in what you actually saw
  rather than what you assumed
- Read **Chapter 8**, from vibes to variables, through the section on how operationalization
  goes wrong
- Next session we take one field note and turn it into a variable a stranger could apply
